Workplaces
Workplace First Aid, CPR & AED
Office and worksite teams
If someone collapses or gets hurt at work, your team should know who takes over, where the AED is and how to get help. Train your responders together at your site.
Start with hands-on First Aid, CPR and AED from HSI or AHA, based on the exact card your employer accepts.
Check how quickly your team can reach medical care. That affects what the federal OSHA first-aid rule requires. OSHA does not endorse training brands.
Tell us about any shifts or work areas that will need their own training time.
Does every employee need the same course?
Not necessarily. Start with the roles named in your emergency plan and confirm employer requirements before training.
Start with the people named in your emergency plan. Check that you have coverage for every area and shift before deciding who needs a seat.

Manufacturing
Manufacturing First Aid, CPR & AED
Manufacturing and plant safety
Train the people who respond first on your production floor. Build the class around your shifts, equipment hazards and the quickest route for EMS to get through the gate.
For floor responders, compare hands-on HSI First Aid/CPR/AED and AHA Heartsaver First Aid CPR AED using your plant’s written requirement.

Check OSHA’s general-industry first-aid rule and, if people face occupational exposure, the bloodborne pathogens standard. A first-aid course does not replace machine-safety or exposure-control training.
Identify when first and second shifts overlap and how a coworker can guide EMS through the gate.
Can one class cover both shifts?
Ask about a shift-overlap session or staggered classes; make sure the plant maintains responder coverage while people train.
Bring your safety lead and responders from each production shift. Leave enough coverage on the floor while the other shift trains.

Warehouses & distribution
Warehouse First Aid, CPR & AED
Warehouses and loading docks
An emergency at the far end of your warehouse can take time to reach. Train responders to work across the floor and dock, get the AED and guide EMS to the right door.
First Aid, CPR and AED usually fits designated dock and floor responders better than clinical BLS. Ask for a session that uses your team’s actual response plan.
Check the federal general-industry first-aid rule and your site’s medical-access plan. Let both inform how many responders you train and where they work.
Tell us where AEDs are mounted and who can open a dock or gate for EMS after hours.
Can we practice a dock emergency?
Tell us the layout and who normally coordinates the response. Keep any exercises away from operating vehicles and active loading areas.
Include shift leads and designated responders from the dock and floor, especially where one team can’t reach the other quickly.

Construction Site First Aid, CPR & AED
Construction and field crews
When a crew moves from job to job, so do the risks and the way EMS gets in. Give your forepersons and designated responders a first-aid plan they can use on site.
Tell us what the contract or safety manager requires. We can help you match a hands-on First Aid/CPR/AED class to the card and documentation your site needs.

If medical care isn’t reasonably accessible, the federal construction rule calls for a trained first-aid person at the worksite. Check the rule’s training and documentation language before you choose a class.
Share the site address or access point, supervisor requirements and how crews rotate between sites.
Is this OSHA 10 or OSHA 30?
No. OSHA Outreach is a separate program and is not replaced by a first-aid card. Verify both items separately if your contract lists both.
Bring forepersons and designated first-aid leads. Tell us which crews move between jobsites so you can plan coverage at each one.

Logging & forestry
Logging Crew First Aid & CPR
Logging and forestry crews
If a worker is hurt far from the road, your crew may be the first help they get. Plan training around remote response, crew roles and the time it takes to bring medical help in.
Send us the logging requirement before booking. We’ll check the proposed first-aid and CPR course against OSHA Appendix B rather than assume a general card is enough.
If your work falls under the federal logging rule, each employee, including supervisors, needs current first-aid and CPR training that meets Appendix B.
Share crew roles, remoteness, transport plans and the exact written Appendix B expectation before booking.
Does a generic CPR card suffice?
No blanket claim is appropriate. Confirm the courses, practical components and paperwork required by your logging operation.
Plan for the whole covered crew, including supervisors. Tell us where crews are spread out and how they reach emergency transport.

Utility Crew First Aid & CPR
Electric utility crews
Plan first-aid coverage around how your utility crews actually work, from remote field jobs to substations, so trained help can get to a coworker quickly.
Tell us what work the crews do and whether they’re in the field or at fixed sites. We’ll discuss first-aid and CPR training alongside, not instead of, your electrical rescue procedures.
If your crew works on or around exposed energized lines or equipment at 50 volts or more, check OSHA’s electric-power rule. It adds first-aid coverage requirements to the general rule.
Distinguish a fixed facility from a mobile crew, and tell us whether your work is construction or operations.
Does the course replace electrical rescue training?
No. Your employer still needs to establish the site-specific rescue, equipment and safety program.
Include field supervisors and designated responders. Separate mobile crews from substation staff when their coverage needs differ.

Confined-space rescue teams
First Aid & CPR for Confined-Space Teams
Industrial rescue teams
Give your designated confined-space rescue team a way to keep its first-aid and CPR credentials current while you handle rescue practice and equipment training separately.
Tell us which standard and credential your program requires. We can quote the first-aid and CPR portion once we have that information.

For covered general-industry spaces, OSHA calls for first-aid and CPR training for designated rescue employees and at least one available team member with current certification. Rescue evaluation and practice are separate.
Send the name and scope of the applicable standard, plus the training and format your employer accepts.
Does this qualify a confined-space rescuer?
No. First Aid/CPR does not replace confined-space rescue evaluation, equipment instruction or practice.
Start with the people named on your rescue team, and check who is available to respond on each shift.

Shipyard First Aid, CPR & AED
Shipyard and vessel repair teams
Help your shipyard responders reach a coworker fast, whether the call comes from a vessel, shop or remote work area. Plan the class around where people work and when they’re on shift.
Tell us what first-aid and CPR card your employer accepts. We can compare hands-on HSI and AHA training for workplace responders.
Check OSHA’s shipyard rule for staffing, response time and its stated exceptions. It also calls for current first-aid and CPR certification for first-aid providers.
Plan for gate access, distance from vessels to the muster point and AED availability away from the main building.
Is this a merchant-mariner course?
Not necessarily. Workplace shipyard first aid and a Coast Guard credential course are separate decisions.
Include first-aid providers from each worksite and shift where you need coverage. Share the fastest access points for EMS.

First Aid Training for Ports & Terminals
Ports and cargo operations
Train the first-aid responders you rely on near the cargo yard, loading areas and waterside work. Keep qualified coverage at the terminal while people train.
Ask for hands-on First Aid, CPR and AED training for your terminal responders, and share what your employer requires on the card.

If your operation falls under OSHA’s marine-terminal rule, at least one person with a valid first-aid certificate must be at the terminal while work is underway. Shipyard and longshoring rules apply to different work.
Identify the terminal access point, shift pattern and how certified coverage will continue during training.
Does this include water rescue?
A first-aid card does not document lifesaving, water rescue or shipboard watch competence.
Start with terminal shift leads and the people designated to provide first aid, then check which work areas each will cover.

Merchant mariners
Merchant Mariner First Aid & CPR
Merchant Mariner Credential applicants
Applying for a Merchant Mariner Credential? Send us your Coast Guard checklist. We’ll help you confirm whether HSINST-203 is the first-aid and CPR course you need.
Ask us to verify the exact HSINST-203 course and approved delivery against your checklist before you pay. If this is instead for your crew’s workplace requirement, tell us that up front.
The Coast Guard lists HSI HSINST-203 for specified Merchant Mariner Credential first-aid and CPR requirements. Check your endorsement separately: this listing does not cover STCW endorsements.
Bring your NMC checklist or the exact credential name so we can distinguish it from STCW Basic Training.
Can I book any First Aid/CPR class?
Don't rely on the course headline alone. Verify the provider, approved delivery, course code and credential checklist first.
This path is for applicants whose checklist calls for first aid and CPR. Tell us which endorsement or credential you’re applying for.

Childcare & preschool
Pediatric First Aid & CPR for Childcare
Childcare and preschool teams
Choosing CPR and First Aid for your childcare staff? Tell us the ages you care for and what your licensing specialist requires. We’ll help you pick a course that covers the right ages.
Ask for pediatric First Aid and CPR, and share the exact title and delivery format your center needs. A course that covers adult first aid alone won’t meet a pediatric first-aid requirement.

For a licensed NC child care center, check DCDEE’s approved course list and format requirements. Its HSI Pediatric First Aid/CPR/AED listing covers applicable child and infant ages, while HSI Pediatric CPR AED or BLS listings cover CPR only. Confirm any required age modules are shown on the card.
Tell us the child age groups, whether staff escort children offsite and which written rule your licensing specialist provided.
Can I use an online-only course?
Do not assume it qualifies. NC center rules restrict distance learning for First Aid, and the approved-program listing distinguishes course formats.
Include direct-care staff and adults who accompany children offsite. Tell us whether your team works with infants, toddlers or older children.

School Staff CPR, AED & First Aid
K–12 campuses
Give your staff a response plan they can practice for the playground, gym or classroom. If your school nurse needs a different card, we can help separate the training before you schedule.
Start with your district’s written requirements. Staff may need First Aid/CPR/AED with pediatric skills, while clinical roles may call for BLS.
Check the district’s rules for each staff role. NC high-school graduation CPR instruction is a separate student requirement; don’t use it to choose a staff credential.
Share the district's written credential and the AED locations in the gym, main office and outdoor areas.
Can teachers and school nurses take the same course?
Often their requirements differ. Send the district's role-specific wording before choosing a single course or two tracks.
Think about teachers, coaches, aides, office staff and school nurses. Bring whichever groups your district requires and distinguish their credentials.

Dental practices
Hands-On BLS for Dental Offices
Dental practices
Need to renew your clinical team’s CPR cards without closing the office for the day? Tell us what your practice needs and we’ll help plan hands-on training around your appointments.
Ask about hands-on AHA BLS or another course that you can verify against the NC rule. If reception or other nonclinical staff need a different card, tell us before combining the group.
Check the NC dental board’s required content and manikin testing. The instructor has to be physically present during the test, so don’t rely on an online-only course.
Share licensed staff roles, office sedation protocol if relevant, and whether nonclinical staff also need general First Aid/CPR/AED.
Can we complete it fully online?
Do not use an online-only class for the NC board’s physically present manikin-test requirement.
Include dentists, hygienists, assistants and office staff as needed. Share which licensed roles are renewing and any separate practice requirements.

Keep patient care moving while your team renews. Tell us which clinicians need BLS, ACLS or PALS and which staff can train together without closing the office.
Start with BLS where your clinic requires it. Add ACLS or PALS only for roles that need adult or pediatric advanced life support.
Check your clinic’s written credential policy for the course, issuer and format it accepts. A BLS card doesn’t replace ACLS, PALS or a separate sedation credential.
List care roles and certification expirations, then identify staff who can train at the same time without closing patient services.
Can we combine clinical and nonclinical staff?
Plan separate tracks if the clinical staff need BLS but other employees need a First Aid/CPR/AED card.
Start with your clinic manager and list clinical and nonclinical staff separately. Group people with the same credential and similar renewal dates.

What about HeartCode?
Confirm whether the facility accepts a blended route, and whether learners have the right online component before arranging hands-on skills.

Restaurant Choking Response, CPR & First Aid
Restaurants and food service

Ask for First Aid, CPR and AED with a focus on choking and common kitchen injuries. Let us know if children regularly dine with you.
Check your workplace and company requirements for first-aid coverage. If your team also needs a food-handler card, plan that training separately.
Plan around a service break and identify who calls EMS and directs responders to the correct entrance.
Can kitchen and dining-room staff train together?

Hotel Guest and Staff CPR & First Aid
Hotels and guest services
An emergency doesn’t wait for your day shift. Train the people who are on hand overnight or away from the front desk, and practice how they’ll get an AED to a guest.
Start with First Aid, CPR and AED for general responders. Tell us separately if pool staff need an aquatic or lifeguard credential.
Check your property’s emergency plan and accepted course. A general workplace first-aid card does not replace lifeguard certification or site-specific procedures.

Tell the instructor your AED model beforehand; use a trainer instead of discharging or removing the real device from service.

CPR, AED & First Aid for Aquatics Teams
Pools and recreation programs

Tell us the exact course your facility accepts for guards and non-lifeguard staff. A general CPR class may fit the front desk while lifeguards need different training.

Is a CPR card enough to work as a lifeguard?
